title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
An AI music generation system was trained on recorded music without obtaining licenses from the rights holders of that music. The failure occurred at the data-collection and model-training stage, before the system was deployed to users. The core issue is a system built for a general purpose, music generation from text prompts, using input data whose legal status was not resolved before training began. Catching it would have required a rights-clearance review of training data before model development, a step the reporting does not establish was taken.

The legal consequences have unfolded across multiple fronts. One major label settled and agreed to a forward-looking licensing arrangement for a new platform. A second major label filed a separate lawsuit alleging the training data included more than 30,000 sound recordings. A court declined to dismiss a copyright class action brought by independent artists. A musicians' union also filed suit related to one of the label settlements. These are allegations and ongoing proceedings, not findings of liability or proof of intent.

What is not established is whether any court has yet ruled that the training constituted infringement, what the financial terms of any settlement are, or how many recordings were actually used in training.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio by reaching licensing agreements. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, including The Temptations' "My Girl." Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs. The financial terms were not disclosed, though UMG stated the agreements reflect their commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies and developing new business models.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, enables users to create original music from text prompts using AI. The startup has attracted millions of users since launching and counts music artist will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz among its backers. This marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label, and artists participating in the new platform will receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed. UMG also announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
